This is Tongyeong ogwandae. 16th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Tongyeong ogwandae · South Korea · 16th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the 16th century alongside the establishment of the navy force in Yongyouung.
It was historically performed by 30 musicians drafted from small islands who practiced for several days before marching in procession from New Year's Eve until the 15th of January.
In the early 20th century, the tradition was revitalized by groups such as Uiheunggye and Nansagye, with Jang jae-bong restoring the form at age 29.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a ceremony to exorcise evil spirits, the performance served as a ritual cleansing for the new year.
Its themes include the portrayal of ordinary people's lives, the satire of the landed gentry, and the ridiculing of domestic issues.
It functions as both a spiritual exorcism and a vehicle for social critique.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The primary dance style is known as 'dutbegi.' The character Malttugi performs an active sword dance that gradually becomes more calm.

The performance is divided into five acts: the lamentation dance of the leper (Mundung-tal), the satirical mockery of noblemen by Malttugi, the predatory movements of the monster Youngno, the monks' dance for jaejagaksi, and the lion dance (sajachum) which concludes with the law of the jungle.
Watch for Dutbegi, Malttugi's Sword Dance, Sajachum.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Processional marching through districts and houses, followed by localized performance of the five stories.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The performance is accompanied by percussion instruments.
The accompaniment is noted for having the characteristic style of the Gyeongsangnam-do province, distinguishing it from other regional five-story mask dances.
Listen for the Percussion instruments.

The music is characterized by a distinct regional percussion style from the Gyeongsangnam-do province. It features rhythmic accompaniment for the 'dutbegi' dance and includes vocal elements such as Buddhist chants used during the exorcism procession.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear specific masks representing the 'five clowns' and other characters like the leper, the monster Youngno, and the lion.
The setting was traditionally the office districts and private houses of Tongyeong during the lunar New Year period.
The lion mask is a unique feature of this specific regional tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures in the restoration and transmission include Jang jae-bong, who restored the dance 90 years ago.
Other designated holders from the 1964 cultural property designation include Oh Jung-du, Kim jin-su, Gu sam-bong, Go young-su, Mun Chang-seob, Kim sam sung, and Yoo ding-ju.
Tongyeong ogwandae is a yeoongna-style mask performance specific to Gyeongsangnam-do.
The dance is a subclass of Korean mask dance (talchum).

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Tongyeong ogwandae is sibling of Pansori: Both are designated as Important Intangible Cultural Properties of Korea.
Tongyeong ogwandae is variant of Sajachum: Tongyeong ogwandae is the only traditional Korean dance currently featuring this lion dance.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The performance includes a ceremony to exorcise evil spirits and involves the chanting of Buddhist prayers by the Junggwandae mask to drive away ghosts.
